news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire forecasts a £54.071m high needs overspend, with its schools grant deficit rising to £54m
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire County Council forecasts a £54.071m overspend this year on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The figure is in the second-quarter financial review, which sits in the papers before the Overview and Scrutiny Management Board. It includes £34.541m that was already planned in the 2026/27 budget. The review says the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, is forecast to go from a £25m deficit to a £54m deficit by March 2027. It also gives a forecast overspend of £51.8m for schools revenue.

The paper says the £22.5m High Needs Stability Grant "does not address the ongoing in-year pressure". It puts the underlying high needs deficit at an increase of around £25m a year. The grant covers 90% of the deficit to 31 March 2026. The council's SEND Reform Plan forecasts a deficit of £57.8m for 2026/27.

On deficits arising after 31 March, the paper says: "Funding arrangements for deficits arising after 31 March are currently unknown". It records that government has said an appropriate and proportionate approach will be taken. Any residual unfunded deficit will need to be considered through future financial planning, the paper says. The reserves statement shows the DSG unusable reserve forecast at a £141.593m deficit in each year from 2027/28 to 2029/30.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - Report to Executive - Review of Financial Performance Q2

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire told of £22.5m grant covering 90% of its schools high-needs deficit after £23.0m overspend
news_drafts.lead:
Government confirmed in October 2026 that Lincolnshire County Council will receive a £22.5m High Needs Stability Grant to cover 90% of its accrued deficit on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The figure appears in the auditors' annual report for 2025/26 on the council's accounts, which goes to the Audit Committee on 16 November.

The council overspent the DSG by £23.0m in 2025/26. The report attributes the overspend principally to the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, and says this reflects a continued increase in children and young people requiring specialist educational support. The school budget deficit stood at £13.4m in 2025/26, against £2.4m in 2024/25.

The report notes that 2025/26 was the first year in which the DSG reserve was forecast to move into a negative position. It says that position was in line with the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy, which forecast a reduction in earmarked reserves. It also says the council had established arrangements to review high needs expenditure to mitigate the DSG deficit.
news_drafts.paper_title: App C - Auditors Annual Report (Lincolnshire County Council) 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire to bring in new special school funding bands from the autumn 2026 term
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire's special schools will be funded under a new banding model from the autumn 2026 term, according to papers for the county's Schools' Forum meeting on 8 October. Banding sets the funding a school receives according to the level of need among its pupils.

The papers, an update on reforms to support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), say the review of the framework has been "progressed and concluded". The new model was developed with special school leaders and finance colleagues. It is meant to line funding up more closely with need, so that banding and funding "more accurately reflect need from the outset".

A key aim, the paper says, is to reduce reliance on exceptional funding arrangements, those that sit outside the standard bands. It also links the change to the long-term financial sustainability of the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The papers give no figures for what the new model will cost or save.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Report to Executive - Review of Financial Performance Q2
findings.headline: Paper states the underlying pressures behind the 2026/27 overspend are expected to continue into 2027/28 and beyond
findings.detail: The paper says the 2027/28 funding base is largely fixed following the multi-year settlement, apart from Council Tax flexibilities. It says the Medium-Term Financial Plan is being updated, with directorate challenge sessions in November. It also says mitigating actions depend on managing demand rather than new funding.
findings.matters: A council stating that its current overspend drivers will carry into the next year, with a largely fixed funding base, is the kind of medium-term signal a finance director or lender would weigh against the MTFP.
findings.figures: Funding base largely established for 2027/28 following the multi-year settlement; MTFP under review
findings.quote: the same underlying financial pressures resulting in the 2026/27 forecast overspend position are expected to continue into 2027/28 and beyond.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Report to Executive - Review of Financial Performance Q2
findings.headline: Resources and Corporate overspend of £1.251m includes a £0.948m carry-forward lost after all 2025/26 service carry forwards were written off
findings.detail: The paper says the directorate entered 2026/27 without its £0.948m underspend carry forward, because all service carry forwards from 2025/26, including overspends and underspends, were written off as part of the approved outturn treatment. It says the directorate's Legal Services and IT transition costs are the main pressures.
findings.matters: A decision to write off carry forwards on both sides at outturn has a direct effect on in-year budgets, and other councils with similar carry-forward rules will want to see how it played out.
findings.figures: Resources and Corporate overspend £1.251m (Quarter 1 £1.506m); lost carry forward £0.948m; Governance deterioration £0.4m
findings.quote: as part of the approved treatment of the 2025/26 outturn, all service carry forwards, including both overspends and underspends, were written off.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Report to Executive - Review of Financial Performance Q2
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing of £437.18m at 3.674% at 30 September 2026, with no new external borrowing expected in 2026/27 and internal borrowing at around £277m
findings.detail: The paper says the borrowing requirement for 2026/27 has fallen from £89.449m at Quarter 1 to £43.482m, and that the council's debt liability benchmark would not need external borrowing this year. It also says long-term rates rose gradually over the period, ending Quarter 2 at around 6.5%, which the paper says is forecast to reduce over the next couple of years.
findings.matters: Lower external borrowing needs combined with a PWLB rate near 6.5% affects the cost of any replacement funding for a LOBO repayment, which is the question finance directors and lenders are asking.
findings.figures: Long-term debt £437.18m at 3.674% (paper also gives 3.67%); borrowing requirement £43.482m (from £89.449m); internal borrowing around £277m; long-term rates around 6.5%; forecast debt at 31 March 2027 £436.53m
findings.quote: At this level, it is not expected that any external borrowing would be required

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Report to Executive - Review of Financial Performance Q2
findings.headline: Treasury review reports a £10m BAE Systems LOBO with a call date of 31/12/2026, and states that if called the council will repay it
findings.detail: The paper says the loan carries a 4% rate and matures on 31/12/2061, and that the council would reject any proposed new rate and repay the £10m if the call is made. The cost of replacement funding is not stated in the paper, though the paper says the possibility has been factored into the year's cash flow. The next call date would be 31/12/2031 if not exercised now.
findings.matters: A LOBO call requires the council to find £10m of replacement funding within weeks, and the replacement cost is what determines whether the council's borrowing position improves or worsens.
findings.figures: LOBO £10m (BAE Systems); coupon 4%; call date 31/12/2026; original maturity 31/12/2061; next call 31/12/2031; debt maturing in year £6.304m
findings.quote: there is a possibility that an existing LOBO loan of £10m from BAE Systems may be called on 31 December 2026 and if so, this will be repaid.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Report to Executive - Review of Financial Performance Q2
findings.headline: Grantham Southern Relief Road has £20.7m rephased into 2027/28 and 2028/29 and completion anticipated in 2028, with a possible cost recovery still to be determined
findings.detail: The paper says the project has been affected by historic programme delays and bridge issues, with the third and final bridge launch scheduled for September and October 2026. It states that the value and timing of any cost recovery related to the bridge issues cannot yet be determined. The scheme budget is £49.056m.
findings.matters: A major road project with a rephased budget, unresolved bridge-related costs and a possible recovery is the kind of scheme a lender or finance director would want to track for both cost and timing.
findings.figures: In-year rephasing £20.7m (£20.7m into 2027/28 and 2028/29); scheme budget £49.056m; completion anticipated 2028
findings.quote: There remains the potential to recover a proportion of costs associated with the bridge issues

daily_post.headline: The auditor has raised a recommendation for structured reporting against the 2026-31 Corporate Plan, after no equivalent performance reporting was presented during 2025/26
daily_post.lead: A peer council would note that performance reporting to committees is being reintroduced against the new plan, which is a governance change.
